questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}=y\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ for $y\ne 0.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{-\operatorname{cos}⁡x},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y=K{e}^{-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.
$$

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}={y}^{2}+1.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={y}^{2}+1 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={y}^{2}+1 \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}+1}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}+1}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}+1}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}y & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{arctan}⁡(y) & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{arctan}⁡(y)=x+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(x+C).
$$

questions.:question/problem:
Find the general solution to the differential equation in part 1 for $T\ne 25.$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $T\,=\,25+K\cdot \,$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        
$\,\,$where $K$ is an arbitrary constant.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we separate variables and integrate both sides with respect to $t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t} & =-0.03(T-25) \\ \frac{1}{T-25}\cdot \frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t} & =-0.03 \\ \int \frac{1}{T-25}\cdot \frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int -0.03\,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{\text{d}T}{T-25} & =-0.03\int \,\text{d}t \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-25| & =-0.03t+C\end{aligned}
$$

This is a perfectly valid general solution. However, if we want to write $T=T(t)$ explicitly, then we can solve for $T.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡|T-25| & =-0.03t+C \\ |T-25| & ={e}^{-0.03t+C} \\ |T-25| & =K\,{e}^{-0.03t}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ is an arbitrary positive constant.

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be both positive and negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =25+K\,{e}^{-0.03t}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2x}{3{y}^{2}}.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2x}{3{y}^{2}} \\ 3{y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3{y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \int 3{y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \int 3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ {y}^{3} & ={x}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
{y}^{3}={x}^{2}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
y=\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}+C}.
$$

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}$ for $y\ne 0$ and $-\frac{\pi }{2}<x<\frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={sec}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y=K{e}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}.

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=x{e}^{-y}.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x{e}^{-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x}{{e}^{y}} \\ {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
{e}^{y}=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C).
$$

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=6x\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}$ for $y\ne 0.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6x\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x\cdot 3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}}\cdot \text{d}y & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}\int {y}^{-2/3}\,\text{d}y & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ {y}^{1/3} & ={x}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
{y}^{1/3}={x}^{2}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
y=({x}^{2}+C)^{3}.
$$

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y′=\frac{5 \left(x - 4\right)^{3}}{y}.$ Assume $x-4>0.$ Take both sign branches on intervals where the radicand is positive and $y\ne 0.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}y′ & =\frac{5 \left(x - 4\right)^{3}}{y} \\ y\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =5 \left(x - 4\right)^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\,\mathrm{d}x & =\int 5 \left(x - 4\right)^{3}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \int y\,\mathrm{d}y & =\int 5 \left(x - 4\right)^{3}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \frac{y^{2}}{2} & =\frac{5 \left(x - 4\right)^{4}}{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\frac{y^{2}}{2}=\frac{5 \left(x - 4\right)^{4}}{4}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y^2 & =\frac{5 \left(x - 4\right)^{4}}{2}+2C \\ y & =\pm\sqrt{\frac{5 \left(x - 4\right)^{4}}{2}+2C} \\ y & =\pm\sqrt{\frac{5 \left(x - 4\right)^{4}}{2}+K}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=2C$ is an arbitrary real constant. Use either sign consistently on each interval where the radicand is positive.

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y′=- 4 e^{- 2 x - y}.$ Work on intervals where the logarithm argument is positive.
questions.:question/worked-solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}y′ & =- 4 e^{- 2 x - y} \\ e^{y}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =- 4 e^{- 2 x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int e^{y}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\,\mathrm{d}x & =\int - 4 e^{- 2 x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \int e^{y}\,\mathrm{d}y & =\int - 4 e^{- 2 x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ e^{y} & =2 e^{- 2 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
e^{y}=2 e^{- 2 x}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
y=\ln{\left(C + 2 e^{- 2 x} \right)}.
$$

The logarithm argument must be positive on the solution interval; $C$ is an arbitrary real constant.

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3{y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2(x+7)\,\text{d}x \\ \int 3{y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int 2(x+7)\,\text{d}x \\ \int 3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y & =\int 2(x+7)\,\text{d}x \\ {y}^{3} & ={(x+7)}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
{y}^{3}={(x+7)}^{2}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
y=\sqrt[3]{{(x+7)}^{2}+C}.
$$

Use the real cube root, on intervals where $y\ne 0.$

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{2x+3}{y}.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{2x+3}{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2x+3}{y} \\ y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x+3\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x & =\int (2x+3)\,\text{d}x \\ \int y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int (2x+3)\,\text{d}x \\ \int y\,\text{d}y & =\int (2x+3)\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & ={x}^{2}+3x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}={x}^{2}+3x+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & ={x}^{2}+3x+C \\ {y}^{2} & =2{x}^{2}+6x+2C \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{2{x}^{2}+6x+2C} \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{2{x}^{2}+6x+K}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=2C.$

questions.:question/problem:
Find the general solution to the differential equation in part 1 for $s\ne 0.$

$s\,=\,($
{{field-1}}$+K)^{-1}$
$\,\,$where $K$ is an arbitrary constant.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we separate variables and integrate both sides with respect to $t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} & =2{s}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} & =2 \\ \int \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{\text{d}s}{{s}^{2}} & =2\int \,\text{d}t \\ -\frac{1}{s} & =2t+C.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a perfectly valid general solution. However, if we want to write $s=s(t)$ explicitly, then we can solve for $s.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{s} & =2t+C \\ s & =-\frac{1}{2t+C} \\ s & =\frac{1}{-2t+K} \\ s & =(-2t+K)^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=-C$ is an arbitrary constant.

questions.:question/problem:
Find the general solution to the differential equation in part 1.

$p\,=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\,$
{{field-1}}$+C)$
$\,\,$where $C$ is an arbitrary positive constant.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we separate variables and integrate both sides with respect to $t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{{e}^{p}} \\ {e}^{p}\cdot \frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t} & =3 \\ \int {e}^{p}\cdot \frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 3\,\text{d}t \\ \int {e}^{p}\text{d}p & =3\int \,\text{d}t \\ {e}^{p} & =3t+C.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a perfectly valid general solution. However, if we want to write $p=p(t)$ explicitly, then we can solve for $p.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{p} & =3t+C \\ p & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3t+C)\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary positive constant.

canonical_example.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y' = \dfrac {x^2}{y}.$
canonical_example.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{y} \\ y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int y\,\text{d}y & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}y^2 = \dfrac{1}{3}x^3 + C.
$$

We can express the solution in the form $y = y(x)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+C \\ {y}^{2} & =\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+2C \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+2C} \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+K}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K = 2C.$
